output:
*Interview with Mademoiselle Lina Ruedi, in the dining room. Second interview of the night.*

MATTHEY: Mademoiselle Ruedi, I am sorry to keep you up. I know it has been a dreadful night for the house. Sit wherever you are comfortable.

MLLE RUEDI: Thank you. I do not know what to do with my hands. I have been sitting in the kitchen since the police came, and I keep thinking someone will tell me it is a mistake. It is not a mistake. He is dead.

MATTHEY: Take your time. Perhaps you could begin with the dinner, and tell me in your own way.

MLLE RUEDI: At dinner, when the temple bell struck nine, the master made everyone show their watches. He does this every year. Mine was exact. Monsieur Félix's was twenty minutes behind. Monsieur Girard's was four minutes behind. The doctor's was two minutes ahead. The master told each of them what was wrong with theirs, and he did not spare anyone.

MATTHEY: And afterwards?

MLLE RUEDI: After dinner I went up and worked beside the master in the atelier, as I always do. When the temple struck ten, the regulator agreed with the bell exactly. I looked at it myself.

MATTHEY: Was he working on anything in particular?

MLLE RUEDI: The repeater. He had been on it four years. It is a minute repeater, so when you press the slide it sounds the time. The low notes are the hours. Each quarter is a doubled note. After the quarter come the high notes, one for each minute past it. He meant it to strike the first minute of the new century. He was very exact about everything, and that was the whole of him.

MATTHEY: When did he send you downstairs?

MLLE RUEDI: He sent me downstairs when the regulator showed twenty past ten. The regulator was running then, and he was well. I did not argue with him. One did not argue with the master about the bench.

MATTHEY: Where did you go?

MLLE RUEDI: I went straight down to the kitchen, and I stayed there with Rosa from when I came down until after the temple struck eleven.

MATTHEY: Did you have your watch with you?

MLLE RUEDI: Yes. In the kitchen I compared my watch with Rosa's clock. Her clock was exactly fifteen minutes fast. She keeps it so on purpose, so that nothing in that house is ever late. I told her it was a good clock for a cook and a poor one for anyone else.

MATTHEY: Did you hear anything while you were in the kitchen?

MLLE RUEDI: We heard Madame's piano. It began at twelve minutes to eleven by the kitchen clock, and it stopped at one minute past eleven by the kitchen clock. I do not know the music well enough to say what it was.

MATTHEY: Do you know of anyone who wished him harm?

MLLE RUEDI: I do not speculate, Inspector. I know his work. I know what he was making and how carefully he made it. Other people's opinions of him are not mine to give.

MATTHEY: Thank you. You have been very clear.

MLLE RUEDI: I regulated my own watch myself, Inspector. I do not let anyone else's hand near it. That is all I can tell you.
